taxonomyNote: NatureServe's name is Saltmarsh Snake (N. clarkii); Rautsaw et al. (2021) question the three subspecies, and Lawson et al. (1991) proposed N. clarkii and N. fasciata as distinct species. The Gulf salt marsh snake is subspecies clarkii.
fieldMarks: Keeled scales in 21 (occasionally 23) rows and a divided anal scale; 38-76 cm, up to 91 cm.
Gulf form typically shows four dark stripes along the back on a lighter body; other forms vary from plain to blotched or banded.
Proportionally smaller head and laterally compressed tail base compared with the banded water snake (N. fasciata, 23 rows).
behavior: Lures small fish by flicking its tongue; eats small fish and fiddler crabs.
Needs fresh water to rehydrate and shifts between saltier and fresher water.
Uses crayfish, fiddler-crab or muskrat burrows, and sometimes shelters under rocks and logs.
habitat: Estuarine brackish and salt marshes with Spartina, Juncus and Salicornia, mangrove swamps, and less often inland freshwater marshes.
range: Brackish coasts of the northern Gulf of Mexico from near Corpus Christi, Texas to Florida (including the Keys) and the Atlantic coast of northern Florida to Volusia County; also northern Cuba.

lookalikes.name: Banded water snake
lookalikes.howToTell: Saltmarsh snake typically has 21 dorsal scale rows, a smaller head and a laterally compressed tail base; banded water snake has 23 rows.

lookalikes.name: Queen snake
lookalikes.howToTell: Queen and Graham's crayfish snakes have 19 or fewer dorsal scale rows; saltmarsh snake has more than 19.

lookalikes.name: Garter snakes
lookalikes.howToTell: Garter snakes have a single anal scale; saltmarsh snake has a divided one.
